text: Jesus was never hurried. He knew His Father makes everything beautiful in its time.
explanation:
On His way to a dying girl's bedside, Jesus stopped to find the woman who had touched His garment, and spoke to her at length. He called her "Daughter," so she'd know she was family, not merely a patient. Then word came that the girl had died. Unruffled, He said, "Do not be afraid; only believe," and raised her up.

We rush and harry ourselves and everyone around us. But "He has made everything beautiful in its time," and that time is kairos, the opportune moment. Jesus never rushed outside it, yet accomplished more than anyone. You can slow down too. Your Father holds the times.

text: A mega storm rose on the lake. One word from Jesus, and there was a mega calm.
explanation:
The Greek says a "great" (megas) windstorm arose, and after Jesus rebuked it, "there was a great calm": megas again. He had slept through the storm itself. What woke Him was His disciples' cry, the way a mother sleeps through thunder but wakes at her baby's whimper.

Having stilled the storm outside, He turned to the storm in their hearts: "Why are you so fearful?" Whatever mega storm you're in, He hears your voice above it. And He can speak one word that brings a calm as great as the storm was.

text: Paul prayed you'd be "strengthened with all might" by the Spirit. For what? "For all patience and longsuffering with joy."
explanation:
You'd expect such power to be for signs and wonders. But Paul prays it for endurance in difficult circumstances and patience with difficult people, with joy. Only the Holy Spirit's strength produces that kind of calm.

It matters. Worry and stress make you irritable with the people you love, who react to your irritation, and the real problem, the care you're carrying, goes untouched. Jesus wasn't easily vexed; people couldn't push His buttons. When you notice irritability rising, don't argue about who's right. Judge the irritation itself, knowing it was dealt with at the cross, and ask the Spirit to strengthen you.

text: Don't let your knowledge of grace stop you from praying. Grace is conscious weakness leaning on God, and that's what prayer is.
explanation:
Some think, "It's all grace, so it'll just happen." But grace means you can't, and He can. Prayer is simply saying so to Him. It isn't hours of religious effort; it's talking to your Father anywhere, about anything: before a difficult conversation with your son, before a decision, when you feel a pain in your body.

We hide our weaknesses and show off our strengths. In God's kingdom it's the other way round: "When I am weak, then I am strong." You can't save a drowning man while he's still thrashing. Stop struggling, bring Him your weakness, and His strength shows up right there.

text: "Whatever things you ask when you pray, believe that you receive them." When do you believe you receive? While you're praying.
explanation:
Not when you see it, not when you feel it, but as you pray. "While they are still speaking, I will hear." God stands outside time; He can set the answer in motion before you've finished asking, because He knows you'll ask.

So pray as one who is near, not far away. You're in Christ, forgiven of all your sins, and God hears. "You do not have because you do not ask." Even John's well-known wish that you would prosper and be in health is, in Greek, a prayer: "I pray that you may prosper." Pray it for your family, and believe as you pray.

text: Shamgar killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad. God loves to work through what looks weak.
explanation:
Ehud was left-handed, which was considered the weak hand, yet that's why he got past the guards to the oppressive king. Shamgar was a farmer with a blunt stick for prodding oxen. Jael used the tent peg and hammer she pitched tents with. Gideon's army was cut from 32,000 to 300, armed with trumpets and clay jars with torches inside.

Your disqualification is God's opportunity to show His strength. "We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellence of the power may be of God and not of us." What's in your hand? Bring it to Him.

text: "The words of the wise are like goads." Your words to your children carry more weight than you think.
explanation:
Parents often think, "They won't listen to me. Their friends and social media matter more." But Scripture notes that David never corrected Adonijah, and Eli never restrained his sons, and both ended badly. Don't hold back from speaking because you assume your words won't land.

Pray first. Then speak simply: a word of correction, of warning, of comfort. Even if they don't look interested, thank the Lord that your words are like goads and have gone in. God gives your words weight. Just as you believe while you're praying, believe while you're speaking.
